title: Neither knows
hook: giving where giver and receiver don't know each other

segments.voice: Yesterday, the top of the ladder, and your line: so they never need to ask. What small step did you take to help someone stand on their own? Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

In the Temple in Jerusalem, Maimonides writes, there was a room called the chamber of secrets. Righteous people would go in quietly and leave something. Poor people from good families would be supported from it, just as quietly. The giver never saw who took. The one who took never saw who gave. Maimonides points to that room when he describes the rung just below the top of his ladder. Today's word is what made the room work.
screen: `THE CHAMBER OF SECRETS.` → `GIVERS GO IN QUIETLY.` → `RECEIVERS GO IN QUIETLY.`

segments.voice: Neither knows. Here is the rung, in plain English: below the highest is one who gives to the poor without knowing to whom he gives, while the poor person doesn't know from whom he takes. Maimonides calls this doing the commandment for its own sake. Turn it four ways. First, what disappears. When neither knows, the giver gets no thanks, no nod at synagogue, no quiet feeling of being owed. And the receiver owes nobody. No awkward meeting in the market, no lowering of the eyes. Both are spared something. Second, for its own sake. Lishmah, in Hebrew. With every reward stripped away, what's left is the gift itself. That's the point. The giver can't be giving to be seen, because no one can see. Third, the room today. Maimonides says something close to this rung is giving into the community's charity fund. But he adds a condition: only if the person in charge is trustworthy, wise, and knows how to manage it properly. Anonymous giving depends on an honest middle. Without one, the secret room is just a dark room. Fourth, why it's not the top. Remember yesterday. The highest rung is personal: a loan, a job, a partnership, help that ends the need. Neither knows is beautiful, but it relieves need rather than ending it. Maimonides keeps both on his ladder, one just under the other. One protects dignity by hiding the giver. The other protects it by making the gift unnecessary. A community needs both kinds of room: the quiet chamber, and the open door to work.
screen: `NO THANKS, NO DEBT.` · `LISHMAH: FOR ITS OWN SAKE.` · `ONLY WITH AN HONEST MIDDLE.` · `JUST UNDER THE TOP RUNG.` · then, large: `NEITHER KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to give anonymously. Settle, and breathe. Think of a way to give today where your name stays out of it. A trusted fund. An unsigned gift. Paying for something no one will trace back to you. Choose one. Now notice what part of you wants to be known for it, even a little. Don't fight that. Just see it, and let it sit beside the gift. Then let the breath carry both. The bell holds the time.
Neither knows. The rung just below the top of Maimonides' ladder: the giver doesn't know who receives, and the receiver doesn't know who gave, like the Temple's chamber of secrets. Today's word.
Your line: neither knows. Today, give one thing with your name left off, and tell no one, not even later. Day one thousand one hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Jews give through community charity funds and collection boxes, called pushkes in Yiddish, so that the giver and the receiver need not know each other.

original.note: Hebrew: the chamber of secrets, a room in the Temple where gifts were given and taken quietly.

trapdoor: what you thought: anonymous giving is the best kind of giving.
what it means: for Maimonides it's very high, just under the top, because it protects the receiver and removes the giver's reward.
what a scholar hears: Matanot Aniyim 10:8, the lishkat chasha'im, and the condition of a trustworthy gabbai for the communal fund.

notes: Matanot Aniyim 10:8 paraphrased: the rung, 'a mitzvah for its own sake', the chamber of secrets, and the condition on the communal fund (kupah) and its administrator.
The chamber of secrets (lishkat chasha'im) is described in Mishnah Shekalim 5:6; please confirm the reference and that 'poor people from good families' fairly renders it.
'In the Temple in Jerusalem' is attributed to Maimonides' own description; please confirm.
howItsDone mentions the Yiddish pushke; please confirm.
Trapdoor floor two says anonymous giving is 'very high'; this is the second rung of eight per 10:7–8.
Editor: cut the invented detail 'nobody stood at the door taking names'; the givers are now 'righteous people' and the receivers 'poor people from good families', closer to 10:8's wording.
